plan.title: Shakshuka: The One-Pan Egg Dish of North Africa
plan.description: Shakshuka is a dish of eggs poached in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce, loved across North Africa and the Middle East. Learn what goes into it, how it is made, and why it is so easy to love.

beats.narration: Eggs, cracked into a bubbling red sauce, cooked right where they land. One pan, a handful of cheap ingredients, and breakfast that people argue about across a whole region. Meet shakshuka.

props.alt: sauce simmering in a frying pan

beats.narration: Shakshuka is a dish of eggs gently poached in a spiced sauce of tomatoes, peppers and onions. It is usually served straight from the pan, with bread for scooping up every last drop.

props.definition: Eggs poached in a spiced sauce of tomatoes, peppers and onions, served in the pan with bread.

beats.narration: It is most strongly linked with North Africa, especially Tunisia, Libya, Algeria and Morocco. From there it spread to Israel and across the Middle East, where families made it their own.

props.title: Where shakshuka is loved
props.caption: North Africa and the Middle East

beats.narration: The word is often said to mean a mixture, which fits. Nothing here is fancy. It is a pantry dish, built from things most kitchens already have, then brought to life with spice.

props.text: Simple ingredients, big flavor, one pan.

beats.narration: Start with ripe red tomatoes, the heart of the sauce. Add colorful bell peppers for sweetness and body. And finish with fresh brown eggs, which cook gently on top of the simmering sauce.
Spices do the rest. Cumin brings earthy warmth, paprika adds color and gentle smoke, and chili brings the heat. Garlic and onion sit underneath, giving the sauce its deep savory base.
First, soften the onions and peppers in oil. Second, stir in garlic and spices. Third, add tomatoes and simmer until thick. Fourth, make small wells and crack in the eggs. Finally, cover and cook.
The common mistake is overcooking. Pull the pan off the heat while the whites are set but the yolks still tremble. They keep cooking in the hot sauce, and a runny yolk is the whole point.

items: Pan off the heat in time

beats.narration: Serve it hot with crusty bread, a scatter of fresh herbs, and maybe some crumbled feta. Tear, scoop, dip. Nobody needs a fork, and nobody leaves the table hungry.

beats.narration: That is the magic of shakshuka. Humble ingredients, one pan, and about half an hour. Tonight, try cracking a few eggs into a simmering tomato sauce, and you will see why it travels so well.

accuracy.reason: Broadly correct, but 'The word is often said to mean a mixture' is hedged and fine, while the Tunisia/Libya/Algeria/Morocco origin claim and the 'about half an hour' timing are not sourced. Origin is debated (Ottoman or Maghrebi) and the script glosses over this.

coverage.reason: The brief wants ingredients with quantities, times and specific steps. The script gives no quantities, no simmer or cook times, and no heat levels. Herbs, feta and the 'tremble' doneness cue are the only extra detail.

structure.reason: Clear order from definition to origin, ingredients, method, doneness and serving. The chapter label 'Why it works' sits oddly over the serving beat.

hook_ending.reason: The opening image of eggs in bubbling sauce is decent, and 'people argue about across a whole region' promises tension that is never paid off. The ending is a generic 'try it tonight' with 'travels so well'.

tone.reason: Warm, accessible and suited to a beginner cooking explainer.

visuals.reason: Good variety (clip, definition, map, gallery, steps, checklist). The map and the steps scene fit the narration. The kinetic text beat is filler.

originality.reason: Mostly generic recipe-video language ('Nothing here is fancy', 'endless comfort', 'nobody leaves the table hungry'). The argument over origin is teased but never explained.

instructions.reason: It is about the right length and in English, but it omits the quantities and times the brief expects. It also frames the dish as 'North Africa' only.

language.reason: Fluent and natural, with only minor filler phrases.
